Gentoo

Pros:

  • You compile everything. This means you can view the source code to insure no backdoors.
  • Since you compile everything, downloads are rather lightweight.
  • You build everything on your system. You know exactly whats in your kernel. You can build just what you need, and it will be even faster than a generic kernel. (Note you can use the generic kernel for Gentoo if you want)
  • Documentation is amazing.

Cons:

  • You aren't going to read the source on everything you are going to install. You'll just emerge everything.
  • Compiling takes forever. Even on SSDs.
  • This is very detailed to install and manage. The only thing I could think is harder is Linux from scratch. Not new user friendly.
  • Keep the documentation on a spare laptop, phone, or tablet. You will need it. Possibly more than you anticipated.

I feel like every GNU+Linux user should install Gentoo at least once. You will know so much about how your system works. Great learning tool.

Ubuntu (default desktop flavour with Unity interface)

Pros:

  • Very popular, lots of community support, other official flavours and separate Linux distros based on it
  • Well supported by video card vendors
  • Good with screen real estate, merges window border with top bar, hide‐able launch bar
  • Long Term Support releases for stability, PPAs for latest versions of whatever you need

Cons:

  • Leaks memory, must be restarted every 2 days or so (log out and back in)
  • Not as good on low end hardware as other desktop environments
  • Canonical refused to remove user data leak until after community uproar
  • Building Mir compositor instead of using community built Wayland, expect problems while they take on this huge task alone
  • Default auto‐hiding scroll bars are confusing
  • Default, MacOS‐style detached drop‐down menus for floating windows are confusing
  • Not as comfortable for people used to Microsoft Windows 95 and derivative interfaces

Ubuntu Official Website

I'm sure I missed things in both categories, but that should be the major points.

Devuan (with Mate):

Pros:

  • As Stable as Debian USED to be

  • Very, VERY efficient on anything < 10 years old

  • No bullshit systemd

  • No clogged up default applications

  • No bullshit command line screwing around

  • No binary logs

  • No Unity

  • No Amazon Search Bar Tie In

  • Not based on Debian upstream fuckery, or Ubuntu downstream fuckery

Cons:

  • Not as intuitive as Linux Mint, Mate edition

  • Not QUITE as pretty as Linux Mint, by default, but you can fix it manually

  • You might be accused of graybearding

  • You have to install the apps you want by hand (very easy)

  • You will have the best, so there's no real possibility of an upgrade

Manjaro: Pros: * Excellent graphical installer, covering everything from partitioning to encryption * Every relevant desktop environment gets a community spin * Terrific theming and integration of the flagship XFCE and KDE editions, same for many of the community spins * Can be as user friendly as anything, if you stick with Octopi or Pamac for package management * Smooth as silk, even on lower end hardware * AUR (Arch User repository) has every open source desktop application known to man

Cons: * Development focus has shifted to testing in recent times, so the "stable" desktop can go a month between kernel, desktop, and package updates.
* Not much emphasis on keeping productivity applications such as LibreOffice as up to date as the rest of the system. * Sometimes inexplicable changes in what gets bundled in the quarterly images, particularly with email clients * Occasional bad timing on kernel updates. 4.4.15-3 got pushed about a day before 4.4.16 came out.

I use the KDE edition. I love MATE as well, have Ubuntu MATE and Ghost BSD installed on older machines. So far, Manjaro strikes the perfect balance for me of being able to stay on an LTS kernel while also having access to an enormous repository without the need for manually adding PPA's.

ArchLinux

Pros:

  • Rolling Release Distribution, meaning you get the newest updates as soon as possible with one simple command pacman -Syu
  • Lightweight, DIY basic installation, you start in a shell environment and customize to your needs from there. This means you chose your Window Manager, Desktop Environment, etc. The system has great flexibility.
  • Excellent Documentation on the Archwiki, it might take some time to read through the important parts, but after installing Arch on my own, I know my system better and finally feel comfortable using and understanding the command line.
  • The Arch User Repository provides a convenient way to install certain packages that would be more difficult to install on other distributions. For example, GTK themes, android studio, TOR browser, Chromium with Netflix plugin.
  • Feels fast with short boot times, performance in games is slightly better for me than it was on Linux Mint

Cons:

  • Installing everything to get the same functionality as a user-friendly distro, takes some previous linux experience, effort, quite a bit of reading on the wiki, trial and error. Install scripts can make this easy, but it kind of defeats the purpose of a DIY distro.
  • Requires manually editing config files for things like getting you graphics driver to work, in which case a typo may lead to errors which you have to then fix from the command line.
  • Although the wiki is very helpful, some sections are outdated or a bit inaccurate and then you may have to improvise a bit.
  • If you use the AUR and can't read code, you are blindly placing trust in strangers to not put malicious software in their repositories (although this could be said about any software really).

Fedora

Pros:

  • All the newest versions of software
  • Great performance on my laptop
  • Pure GNOME (Very very little customization - afaik nothing other than changing the default desktop)
  • Wide array of packages available by default
  • frequent updates to software packages

Cons:

  • Some of the newest software versions have had minor bugs
  • Important codecs aren't available by default - it takes an annoying 2 mins to google for the command to enable the repos with the illegally free codecs
